results.ask: How do nonfiction writers usually handle mentioning a study like this in a popular book?
results.watch: R1 common practice and variation; no invented citation (editorial stance).
results.reply:
The most common split is about where the sourcing lives. In popular nonfiction, a lot of writers name the researcher and the institution right in the sentence — it gives the finding a face and a place, and readers tend to trust a claim with a name attached. Others keep the body text clean and push everything to endnotes that are keyed to a page number and a phrase rather than marked with superscript numbers in the text, so the reading isn't interrupted but anyone who wants the citation can find it. Both are ordinary. The first costs you a little speed in the sentence; the second means a curious reader has to go looking.

A second common move, when the finding is one most readers have already absorbed secondhand: writers give one concrete detail of what was actually done — the task, roughly how many people — because a specific image makes the later reversal land harder than a general description would. The cost is a sentence or two of room, and specific numbers can date a book.

On contested findings in particular, the replication trouble is now usually handled in the main text rather than tucked into a note, on the reasoning that the failure to replicate *is* the story rather than a technical footnote to it. Some writers name how many replications and with what result; some keep it general and let the notes carry the detail.

Practice differs by house and by moment. Journalism-derived books tend to name sources in text; some science imprints want fuller apparatus; a few publishers now put the source list online instead of in the back. I can't give you a firm figure or requirement — it varies between publishers and shifts over time.

results.watch: R1 common practice and variation; no invented citation (editorial stance).
results.reply:
Mostly it comes down to how much of the citation apparatus they put in the sentence itself versus push to the back of the book.

In trade nonfiction the common pattern is to keep the running text light — a phrase like "a series of studies in the late 1990s," maybe a researcher's name if that person is going to recur — and let an endnote carry the journal, year and authors. Many trade publishers key those notes by page number and a snippet of text rather than superscript numbers, on the reasoning that visible note markers make a page look like a textbook. Books that sit closer to science journalism or to academic-trade crossover often do use superscripts, and some popular-science writers name the lead researcher in the body because it gives them a person to follow rather than a finding to report. All of these are live practices; what a given publisher wants varies, and house style changes over time.

The other thing writers decide is how much of a finding's *status* goes in the body. Since the replication arguments of the last decade or so, it's become fairly common in popular science to say in the text itself that later attempts to repeat a result didn't hold, rather than tuck that into a note — the argument being that a note only reaches the reader who goes looking, and a reader who stops at the main text would otherwise carry away the original claim intact. Your passage does that work in the body already, which is its own choice with its own effect: the reader meets the doubt at the same moment as the claim.

What each costs: naming names, dates and institutions buys checkability and a sense of specificity, and spends pace and attention. Leaving them out keeps momentum and asks the reader to extend trust — which some readers extend easily and some don't.

results.ask: How do nonfiction writers usually handle mentioning a study like this in a popular book?
results.watch: R1 common practice and variation; no invented citation (editorial stance).
results.reply:
There's no single practice, but a few recurring ones in trade nonfiction, each with a different cost.

**Naming the work in the body.** Many writers put a researcher, institution, and year into the sentence itself — the lab, the year, sometimes the journal. It gives a reader something to hold and makes the claim checkable without turning to the back. It costs pace, and it can quietly overstate one lab's ownership of an idea that several groups were working on. The opposite choice — an unattributed gesture at a body of work, which is what your second sentence does — keeps momentum and avoids implying that one paper settled anything, at the cost of a reader who wants to look it up having to go to the notes to do it.

**Describing the experiment rather than citing it.** A common move is one concrete scene — what the subjects were asked to do, what was measured — in place of any apparatus. Readers tend to remember a procedure better than a finding. The risk is that a vivid single study becomes, in the reader's mind, the whole evidence base, which is awkward if your next beat is that the evidence base didn't hold.

**Where the citation lives.** Most US and UK trade publishers now prefer unnumbered endnotes keyed by page number and a catchphrase, so the page stays clean. Crossover and university-press books more often use superscripts or numbered notes. This genuinely varies by publisher and has shifted over time; it's usually settled in copyediting, not drafting, so it's not something you need to decide now.

**Handling the replication problem.** Since roughly the mid-2010s it's become ordinary rather than unusual for popular books to say outright that a famous result didn't replicate. Writers differ in how much weight they give it: some name a specific multi-lab attempt and a number, which is harder to wave away but drags the reader into methodology; some keep it general, as a shift in the field's confidence, which is faster but leaves the claim resting on the writer's authority. Hedged verbs — *seemed to*, *was taken to show* — are the usual way of marking that a finding was once believed without endorsing it.

**Naming the bestsellers.** Some writers name the books they're correcting; some don't. Naming is specific and gives the reader a target, but it dates the book and invites a fight. Not naming keeps the sentence moving and avoids making the passage about particular authors.

results.ask: What order do editors usually revise a chapter in?
results.watch: R1 describes common practice as practice, not a required sequence.
results.reply:
Most editors work from the largest decisions down to the smallest, on the simple logic that there's no point polishing a sentence you might cut.

Roughly, that looks like: first, does this chapter need to exist, and does it do what the book needs here — what changes by the end, what the reader learns, whether it earns its place. Then the shape inside it: the order of events, where it starts and stops, what's scene and what's summary, whether anything is doing the same job twice. Then who's telling it and how close we are to them, which is where point of view and the handling of time usually get settled. Then line work: rhythm, word choice, clarity, cutting what's slack. Then the surface pass, last, when nothing more is going to move.

What this order does for a reader is mostly invisible — it just means the book doesn't have beautifully written passages that shouldn't be there, or a chapter that was smoothed into blandness before anyone asked what it was for. The cost is that it can feel like working in the dark for a long while; some writers find that the big questions only become answerable *through* sentence-level work, because they don't know what the chapter is until they've heard how it sounds. Those writers often reverse parts of it, or loop.

Practice does differ. Commercial fiction houses tend to formalise the stages into separate editorial passes with different people doing each. Literary publishing more often blurs the middle stages into one long conversation between writer and editor. In poetry and short prose the whole distinction thins out, because the shape and the sentence are nearly the same thing. And plenty of working writers don't use discrete stages at all — they revise one chapter to something near-final before moving on. None of that is a rule, and no editor I know of applies the sequence rigidly.
